speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** Can I deduct home-office expenses if I work from home?

**Jordan:** Assuming we’re talking about U.S. federal income tax, it depends on whether you’re self-employed or a W-2 employee. Most W-2 employees can’t deduct home-office expenses on their federal return, even if their employer requires them to work from home. State rules may differ.

**Alex:** What if I’m self-employed?

**Jordan:** You generally need to use a clearly identifiable part of your home **regularly and exclusively** for business. It doesn’t have to be a separate room, but a kitchen table you also use for meals usually won’t qualify. Your home office can qualify as your principal place of business if you use it for administrative or management work and have no other fixed location where you do substantial work of that kind. Special rules apply to daycare and certain inventory storage.

**Alex:** How do I calculate the deduction?

**Jordan:** There are two methods. The **simplified method** is $5 per square foot of qualifying space, up to 300 square feet—a maximum of $1,500 before any income limitation. The **actual-expense method** generally lets you deduct the business share of costs like rent, utilities, and insurance, plus qualifying expenses that relate only to the office. If you own your home, depreciation may also factor in and can affect your taxes when you sell.

**Alex:** So the simplified method is easier, but not necessarily better?

**Jordan:** Exactly. Compare both if you qualify, and keep records of the space you use and how you calculated the deduction.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** What if I have a W-2 job and also freelance from home?

**Jordan:** You can claim a home-office deduction for qualifying freelance use, but not for your W-2 work. If you use the same desk for both, don’t assume you can deduct half the cost based on hours. The space has to qualify for the business you’re claiming it for. A clearly identifiable area used regularly and only for freelancing makes that distinction easier.

**Alex:** Where do I claim it?

**Jordan:** If you’re a sole proprietor, the deduction goes on Schedule C. You generally use Form 8829 to calculate it under the actual-expense method; with the simplified method, you calculate it directly on Schedule C. One difference worth checking: eligible expenses you can’t deduct because of the income limit may carry forward under the actual-expense method, but an unused simplified deduction doesn’t.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** If I’m just starting out and my freelance business doesn’t turn a profit, can the home-office deduction offset my W-2 wages?

**Jordan:** No. The home-office deduction generally can’t create or increase a loss from your freelance business. Your W-2 wages don’t increase that limit. Under the actual-expense method, though, eligible expenses you couldn’t deduct may carry forward to a later year, subject to that year’s limit.

**Alex:** Does that mean I can’t deduct my freelance expenses at all if my desk doesn’t qualify?

**Jordan:** No. The home-office rules apply to the cost of using your home. You can still generally deduct ordinary and necessary freelance expenses, like software or supplies, on Schedule C. If you use something for both freelancing and personal or W-2 work, deduct only the portion attributable to freelancing and keep records of how you calculated it.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** So my other freelance expenses could offset my W-2 wages even if my home-office expenses can’t?

**Jordan:** Potentially, yes. If you’re running a business for profit and your deductible freelance expenses exceed your freelance income, the resulting Schedule C loss can generally offset W-2 wages on your federal return, subject to applicable loss limits. The home-office deduction has its own limit: it generally can’t create or increase that loss.

**Alex:** What if I bought software before I started taking clients?

**Jordan:** The key is when your business began operating, not when you got your first client. If you were already operating, the software may qualify as a regular business expense. If you bought it while still setting up, it may be a startup cost, which follows different deduction rules.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** How do I deduct startup costs?

**Jordan:** For U.S. federal taxes, in the year your business begins operating, you can generally deduct up to $5,000 in qualifying startup costs. That $5,000 limit drops dollar for dollar once your total startup costs exceed $50,000. You generally spread any remaining costs over 180 months, starting in the month the business begins.

**Alex:** So does my software subscription count?

**Jordan:** A subscription you used to prepare for launch may qualify as a startup cost if it would otherwise be an ordinary and necessary business expense. A subscription you use once you’re operating is generally a regular Schedule C expense to the extent it’s used for freelancing. Purchased software can follow different rules, so keep the invoice and note when and how you started using it.

**Alex:** Can I deduct the subscription even if my home office doesn’t qualify?

**Jordan:** Yes. The software expense is separate from the cost of using your home. You don’t need a qualifying home office to deduct the eligible business portion.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** What if my subscription covers a full year, and I launch halfway through?

**Jordan:** Don’t classify the whole payment as a startup cost just because you paid before launch. The portion attributable to preparing to open may qualify as a startup cost, while the portion attributable to operating the business is generally a regular business expense. The timing of the deduction can depend on your accounting method and the rules for prepaid expenses. Keep the invoice, the subscription dates, and a note explaining when you began operating and how you allocated the cost.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** If I paid $240 for a calendar-year subscription and launched July 1, would that be $120 in startup costs and $120 in operating expenses?

**Jordan:** That’s a reasonable allocation if the subscription cost was spread evenly over the year and you used it solely for freelancing—first to prepare for launch, then to run the business. The first $120 would go into your pool of qualifying startup costs, and the second $120 would generally be a Schedule C operating expense. That split classifies the costs; your accounting method and the prepaid-expense rules determine when you can deduct them.

**Alex:** What if I also used it for my W-2 job?

**Jordan:** Exclude the W-2 and personal use before figuring the freelance deduction. If your freelance use differed before and after launch, estimate the business share separately for each period and keep a short note showing how you arrived at it.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** Suppose my freelance use was 25% before launch and 75% after. What would I deduct?

**Jordan:** Using the $120-per-half split, you’d allocate **$30 to startup costs** ($120 × 25%) and **$90 to operating expenses** ($120 × 75%). The remaining $120 isn’t deductible on Schedule C because it wasn’t for freelancing. The $30 goes into your startup-cost total, and the $90 is generally a Schedule C expense, subject to the timing rules we discussed. Keep the invoice and a note explaining how you estimated each percentage.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** So can I deduct the full $120 in the year I launch?

**Jordan:** Generally, yes, if the $90 operating expense is deductible that year under your accounting method and prepaid-expense rules, and the $30 fits within your immediate startup-cost deduction. The $5,000 startup limit applies to **all** your qualifying startup costs combined, not to each purchase. Any qualifying startup costs you can’t deduct immediately are generally spread over 180 months starting in the month you launch.

**Alex:** And the home-office income limit doesn’t apply to the software?

**Jordan:** Right. The software is a separate business expense. You don’t need a qualifying home office to deduct the freelance share.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** Could the software expense reduce my home-office deduction if I do qualify?

**Jordan:** Yes. The home-office income limit generally takes other freelance expenses into account first. If you deduct the full $120 this year, it generally reduces the income available for the home-office deduction by $120. If that leaves no income available, you generally can’t take a home-office deduction that year. It’s the home-office deduction that’s limited, not the software expense.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** Can you show me what that looks like in dollars?

**Jordan:** Suppose you have $300 of freelance income left after all other business expenses, but before deducting the $120 in software costs. After the software deduction, you have $180 left. If your simplified home-office deduction would otherwise be $250, you can claim only $180 that year.

**Alex:** Can I deduct the remaining $70 next year?

**Jordan:** Not under the simplified method. Under the actual-expense method, eligible home-office expenses disallowed by the income limit can generally carry forward and be deducted in a later year when you use the actual-expense method, subject to that year’s limit.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** What if I switch to the actual-expense method next year? Can I recover that $70?

**Jordan:** No. You can switch methods from year to year, but switching won’t bring back the $70 you couldn’t claim under the simplified method. If you’re comparing methods for this year, calculate your actual expenses separately—the $70 is the unused part of the simplified deduction, not a measure of your actual expenses.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** What if I use actual expenses this year, switch to simplified next year, and then switch back?

**Jordan:** Eligible actual expenses you couldn’t deduct because of the income limit can generally carry forward. You can’t use that carryforward in a year when you choose the simplified method, but you can generally use it when you switch back to actual expenses, subject to that year’s income limit.

**Alex:** So the simplified year pauses the carryforward rather than wiping it out?

**Jordan:** Exactly. The key is where the unused amount came from: eligible **actual expenses** can carry forward, but an unused **simplified deduction** never does.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** Is there a downside to switching to the simplified method for a year?

**Jordan:** You can’t use your actual-expense carryforward that year, even if you have enough freelance income to absorb it. But the simplified method may still give you a bigger deduction for that year. Compare the simplified amount with what you could actually deduct under the actual-expense method, including any eligible carryforward and applying the income limit to both.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** If both methods give me the same deduction this year, is there a reason to pick one over the other?

**Jordan:** Yes. If you use the simplified method, you generally have less paperwork and preserve any existing actual-expense carryforward for a later year. The trade-off is that you can’t carry forward any unused simplified deduction or build a new actual-expense carryforward for that year.

**Alex:** Does it matter if I own my home?

**Jordan:** It can. With the simplified method, you don’t deduct home-office depreciation for that year, so there’s no depreciation for that year to account for when you sell. It doesn’t erase depreciation from earlier years. If the deductions are the same, weigh the simpler recordkeeping against whether using or building an actual-expense carryforward would be more useful to you.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** What if both methods give me a $180 deduction, but the actual-expense method leaves $70 of eligible expenses I can’t deduct this year?

**Jordan:** Then the actual-expense method gives you the same $180 now and generally lets you carry the $70 forward. You can use it in a later year when you choose the actual-expense method and have enough business income under that year’s limit. If you choose the simplified method this year, you don’t create that $70 carryforward.

**Alex:** So actual expenses are the better choice?

**Jordan:** Not necessarily. The $70 is a potential future **deduction**, not $70 in tax savings. If you’re unlikely to use it, the simpler paperwork may be worth more to you. And if you own your home, check how much depreciation you’d be allowed under the actual-expense method—it can affect your taxes when you sell.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** How much could that $70 carryforward actually save me?

**Jordan:** If you deduct the full $70 in a later year and your marginal federal income tax rate is 22%, that’s about **$15 in federal income tax savings**. It may also reduce self-employment tax. But you’ll only get the benefit if you use the actual-expense method in a later year and have enough business income to deduct it.

**Alex:** What would you pick?

**Jordan:** If both methods give you $180 now and the only extra benefit is a $70 carryforward, I’d lean toward the simplified method if tracking actual expenses would be a hassle. If you already have the records and expect to use the carryforward soon, actual expenses may be worth it. If you own your home, factor in how any depreciation you deduct could affect your taxes when you sell.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** What records should I keep if I go with the simplified method?

**Jordan:** Keep a sketch or measurements of the qualifying workspace, a note on when you started using it for freelancing, and your deduction calculation. You don’t need to track rent or utility bills *for the simplified deduction*, but keep records for separate business expenses, like the software invoice and your freelance-use calculation. If you already have an actual-expense carryforward, keep the prior Form 8829 so you can track it if you switch back.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** How long should I keep those records?

**Jordan:** For U.S. federal taxes, generally at least three years from the date you filed the return or its due date, whichever is later. Keep records supporting an actual-expense carryforward until the retention period has passed for the return on which you finally use it. If you claimed home-office depreciation in an earlier year, keep those records through the retention period for the return reporting the sale of your home.

**Alex:** What if I move or change workspaces midyear?

**Jordan:** Note when each space started and stopped qualifying, and keep the measurements for both. The simplified method accounts for changes in qualifying square footage during the year, so don’t just use the size of your office on December 31.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** Can I use the simplified method for both homes if I move?

**Jordan:** No. If you used offices in two different homes during the same tax year, you can elect the simplified method for only one home. You can use actual expenses for the other home if the office qualifies. If you just switched workspaces within the *same* home, use the simplified method’s monthly square-footage calculation to account for the change.

**Alex:** What would that look like?

**Jordan:** Say you used a qualifying 120-square-foot office from January through June, then moved to a different home. If you choose the simplified method for the first home, average its qualifying area over all 12 months: 120 × 6 ÷ 12 = 60 square feet. At $5 per square foot, that’s **$300 before the income limit**. For the second home, you’d calculate any deduction using actual expenses for the qualifying period.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** What if I move in the middle of June? Does June count for the first home?

**Jordan:** For the simplified method, count a month only if you had at least **15 days of qualifying use** in that home. If your 120-square-foot office qualified for 15 days in June, June counts and the deduction is **$300 before the income limit**. If it qualified for only 14 days, June doesn’t count: 120 × 5 ÷ 12 = 50 square feet, for **$250 before the income limit**.

**Alex:** Does that 15-day rule also apply to the second home if I use actual expenses there?

**Jordan:** No. That rule is for calculating square footage under the simplified method. For the second home, base the actual-expense deduction on eligible costs and the period the office qualified. Keep a note of when each office started and stopped qualifying.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** If my first office qualifies through June 15 and my second office starts qualifying June 16, can I deduct both for June?

**Jordan:** Yes, assuming both offices otherwise qualify. If you use the simplified method for the first home, its 15 qualifying days are enough to count June in the square-footage calculation. For the second home, use actual expenses and allocate eligible costs to the qualifying business use from June 16 onward. The 15-day rule doesn’t apply to that calculation, and you can’t count the same expense twice. Both deductions are subject to the applicable business-income limit.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** Do I get a separate business-income limit for each home?

**Jordan:** Not a fresh limit for each. If both offices serve the same freelance business, allocate the business’s gross income and non-home-office expenses between the two homes on a reasonable basis. Then apply the home-office income limit to each calculation using its share. Don’t use the full year’s business income to support both deductions.

**Alex:** What’s a reasonable way to split them?

**Jordan:** Start with what you can trace to each period. For example, if you bought supplies for a project you worked on entirely before the move, assign that cost to the first period. For shared costs, like a yearlong software subscription, use a reasonable allocation that reflects business use. Keep a short note explaining your split. The 15-day rule determines whether June counts for the first home’s simplified square-footage calculation; it doesn’t determine where June’s income or expenses go.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** What if I finish a project before I move but the client pays me afterward?

**Jordan:** If you use cash-basis accounting, you generally report the payment in the year you receive it. But if the work and payment fall in the same tax year, don’t automatically assign the payment to the second office just because it arrived after the move. For the home-office income-limit calculation, assigning it to the first office is generally reasonable if you did all the work there. If you worked on the project in both offices, use a reasonable split, such as documented hours worked in each. That allocation doesn’t change when you report the income on Schedule C.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** What if the client doesn’t pay me until January of the next year?

**Jordan:** If you’re a cash-basis taxpayer, you generally report the payment in January’s tax year, assuming it wasn’t already available to you in December. You don’t move it back to the prior year to increase the deduction for your first home office.

**Alex:** Can I still get a tax benefit from expenses I couldn’t deduct for the first office?

**Jordan:** That depends on the method you used for that office. If you used the **simplified method**, any deduction you lost to the income limit is gone. If you used the **actual-expense method**, eligible disallowed expenses generally carry forward. You may be able to deduct them even after moving, in a year when you use the actual-expense method for a qualifying office and have enough business income under that year’s limit.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** Can the January payment help me use that carryforward even though I earned it at the old office?

**Jordan:** Potentially. For a cash-basis business, the payment generally goes on Schedule C in the year you receive it, assuming it wasn’t available to you earlier. But reporting it that year doesn’t automatically mean the full payment counts toward the new office’s deduction limit. If you earned income from business activities conducted both in and outside the qualifying office, use a reasonable allocation based on where you did the work and keep a note explaining it. You can use the carryforward only to the extent the actual-expense calculation allows it.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** So if the January payment is my only freelance income, should I assume I can use the $70 carryforward?

**Jordan:** No. Report the payment on Schedule C for the year you receive it, but don’t automatically treat it as income attributable to the new office just because you received it there. If you did all the work at the old office, the payment may not give you any room under the new office’s deduction limit.

**Alex:** What happens to the $70 if I still can’t deduct it?

**Jordan:** If it’s an eligible carryforward from the actual-expense method, it generally carries forward again. Keep the earlier Form 8829 and your allocation notes so you can claim it in a later year when you use actual expenses and have enough income under that year’s limit.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** Does the $70 carryforward expire after a certain number of years?

**Jordan:** Generally, there’s no fixed expiration period for an eligible federal home-office carryforward from the actual-expense method. It can carry forward until you have a qualifying home office, use the actual-expense method, and have enough income under that year’s limit. If you never meet those conditions again, you may never get to deduct it.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** What if I stop freelancing and only work my W-2 job?

**Jordan:** You generally can’t use the $70 carryforward to offset your W-2 wages. If you stop freelancing permanently, the carryforward may never give you a tax benefit. If you’re only taking a break, keep the old Form 8829 and supporting records so you can check whether you can use it when you resume the business.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** What if I keep freelancing but rent a desk at a coworking space instead?

**Jordan:** You generally can’t use the $70 home-office carryforward in a year when you don’t have a qualifying home office. But the coworking fee is a separate expense: you can generally deduct the freelance portion on Schedule C as an ordinary and necessary business expense. Keep the old Form 8829 in case you qualify for the home-office deduction again.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** Can I deduct the coworking fee and still claim a home-office deduction if I use both?

**Jordan:** Potentially. The coworking fee is a separate Schedule C expense, but your home office still has to qualify on its own. If you’re relying on the rule for administrative or management work, you can still qualify if you regularly and exclusively use the home office for that work and don’t do substantial administrative or management work at another fixed location. Meeting clients or doing project work at the coworking space doesn’t, by itself, disqualify your home office.

**Alex:** What does that mean for my $70 carryforward?

**Jordan:** If your home office qualifies and you use the actual-expense method, you may be able to use it. But the deductible coworking fee generally reduces the business income available under the home-office limit, so it could leave less room to deduct the carryforward this year.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** Can you show me how the coworking fee affects the $70?

**Jordan:** Say you have $100 of freelance income left after other business expenses, but before deducting a $60 coworking fee. That leaves $40 under the home-office income limit. If your home office qualifies, you use actual expenses, and no current-year home-office expenses take up that room, you could deduct $40 of the carryforward and carry the remaining $30 into a later year.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** What if I also have $25 in current-year home-office expenses?

**Jordan:** It depends on the type of expense and where it falls in Form 8829’s deduction order. If the $25 is for current operating expenses, like utilities, and the $70 carryforward is also for operating expenses, the $40 limit applies to the combined $95. You’d deduct **$40** this year and carry **$55** forward. If the carryforward is for depreciation instead, operating expenses generally come first.

**Alex:** What if the $60 coworking fee uses up all the income I have left?

**Jordan:** You can generally still deduct the business portion of the coworking fee on Schedule C. But if it leaves no room under the home-office income limit, you won’t use any of the $70 carryforward that year. Keep Form 8829 and your supporting records for a later year.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** So if I have no room this year, does the $25 get added to the $70?

**Jordan:** Yes, if the $25 is an otherwise deductible home-office operating expense and you use the actual-expense method for a qualifying office. If the income limit blocks both amounts, you’d carry forward **$95**. If the $70 is a depreciation carryforward, track it separately from the $25 in operating expenses on Form 8829.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** What if I choose the simplified method this year instead?

**Jordan:** If there’s no income left under the home-office limit, you get no simplified deduction for the year. Your existing **$70 actual-expense carryforward** stays available for a later year when you use the actual-expense method and have enough qualifying business income. But the **$25 in current-year operating expenses** won’t be added to it.

**Alex:** So both methods give me zero this year, but actual expenses could leave me with $95 to carry forward instead of $70?

**Jordan:** Exactly, assuming the $25 is otherwise deductible and your office qualifies. The difference is **$25 in potential future deductions**, not $25 in tax savings.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** Would you use actual expenses just to preserve that extra $25?

**Jordan:** If I already had the records and expected enough freelance income to use the carryforward, I’d lean toward actual expenses. But at a 22% marginal federal income tax rate, that extra $25 deduction would save only **$5.50 in federal income tax** if you eventually use it, before any effect on self-employment tax. If tracking actual expenses would be a hassle, the simplified method may be worth it: you’d still preserve the existing $70 carryforward.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** What if I file with the simplified method and later realize I should’ve used actual expenses?

**Jordan:** You generally can’t switch methods for that tax year after electing the simplified method on a timely filed original return. You can choose actual expenses next year, but that won’t let you recover the extra $25 from this year. Your existing $70 carryforward would still be available, subject to the usual limits.

**Alex:** So I should compare both before I file?

**Jordan:** Yes. In your example, both methods give you a $0 deduction this year. The decision is whether documenting the actual expenses now is worth preserving an extra $25 deduction you might use later.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** If I go with actual expenses, should I file Form 8829 even though my deduction is zero?

**Jordan:** Yes. In your example, use Form 8829 to calculate the $0 deduction and document the **$95 carryforward**. Keep a copy with your expense records. If the $70 is a depreciation carryforward, track it separately from the $25 in operating expenses rather than treating the whole $95 as one category.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** Where do I enter the carryforward next year?

**Jordan:** If you use the actual-expense method again, take the carryover amounts from Part IV of this year’s Form 8829 and enter them in the corresponding carryover fields in Part II of next year’s form. Keep operating expenses separate from depreciation and other excess casualty losses, as the form directs. The **$95 is a carryforward, not an automatic deduction**: next year’s Form 8829 determines how much you can deduct on Schedule C.

**Alex:** And if I use the simplified method next year?

**Jordan:** Don’t include the $95 in the simplified calculation. Keep this year’s Form 8829 so you have the amounts when you next use the actual-expense method.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** If I use the simplified method for two years, which form do I look back to when I switch back?

**Jordan:** Use Part IV of the **last Form 8829 you filed for that business**, even if it’s two years old. Enter the carryforward in the corresponding fields on your new Form 8829, keeping the expense categories separate. The simplified years neither reduce the $95 nor add to it. Your new Form 8829 determines how much you can deduct that year.
